Reproducing Liu, Nair et al. (2024) from dandiset 001097¶

Paper: Liu M, Nair A, Coria N, Linderman SW, Anderson DJ (2024). Encoding of female mating dynamics by a hypothalamic line attractor. Nature 634, 901-909. doi:10.1038/s41586-024-07916-w. Open access (CC BY, PMC11499253); the full text, Methods and Extended Data legends were used.

Data: DANDI:001097, version 0.260624.0330, streamed from the archive.

Why this version. The paper cites the dandiset by accession number only. Of the three published versions, 0.240814.1849 holds only the two per-mouse files; 0.260531.0005 and 0.260624.0330 hold the same 107 files with the same asset identifiers (shown below). The most recent, 0.260624.0330, is pinned. The two per-mouse files are byte-identical across all three versions.

Code read: neuralcomputation/hypothalamic-dynamics at commit 28fee70, which the dandiset links. It holds demonstration notebooks that fit rSLDS models with the ssm package (lindermanlab/ssm at commit eb6c8aa) to one mating session (the per-mouse file of m541), and loading, smoothing, autocorrelation and plotting functions. It does not hold the code for the paper's figures. Where it settles a choice the Methods leave open (smoothing, the autocorrelation half-width, which cells count as weighted) it is followed here, and the helper module says so.

What can and cannot be tested¶

The dandiset holds the imaging and annotations of the 15 receptive mice of Figures 2 and 3, the oestrogen-injected cohort of Figure 5i-l (42 trials where the paper has 50), natural-cycle and ovariectomy series, and male-inhibition sessions. It holds no fitted rSLDS models apart from the per-cell weights of two mice.

The rSLDS cannot be refit here. The ssm package is a Cython extension installed from GitHub that does not build in the registry's locked environment, and with the authors' settings (3 states, 2 dimensions, 150 iterations of Laplace EM) one fit of a 10,000-frame session takes about 7.5 minutes (10 iterations took 30 s), so the 90 or so fits the claims need would take hours. (These timings, and the stand-in below, were measured while preparing this attempt and are not run in this notebook.) A single linear dynamical system, tried as a stand-in while preparing this attempt, fitted rotations with two equal time constants in 14 of the 15 receptive sessions, so it cannot separate an integration dimension from the others and is not a test of the claims. Claims that need new rSLDS fits are blocked.

Versions of the dandiset¶

The paper cites the dandiset by accession number only, with no version. Three versions are published. The comparison below lists, for each, the files and their asset identifiers.

In [2]:

Load the data and check it against its description¶

Every file's annotations are read, and the traces of the sessions the analysis uses: the 15 receptive sessions, the oestrogen-injected cohort, the natural-cycle days of the two mice with deposited rSLDS weights, and a few sessions needed to check duplicates.

In [3]:
files = tables[vmhvl.VERSION]
sessions_t = files[files.session.notna()].copy()
annotations = vmhvl.load_many(sessions_t.path.tolist(), neural=False)
sessions_t["n_frames"] = [annotations[p].n_frames for p in sessions_t.path]
sessions_t["n_cells"] = [annotations[p].n_cells for p in sessions_t.path]
sessions_t["kind"] = [annotations[p].kind for p in sessions_t.path]
sessions_t["female_annotated"] = [annotations[p].has_female() for p in sessions_t.path]
sessions_t["receptive"] = [annotations[p].receptive() for p in sessions_t.path]

receptive_paths = sessions_t[sessions_t.experiment == "receptive"].path.tolist()
oestrogen_paths = sessions_t[sessions_t.experiment == "oestrogen-injected (7 days)"].path.tolist()

    ("sub-m764_ses-WT_3d_mating_d1_ecephys+behavior.nwb", "sub-m764_ses-ovx_primed_receptive_mating_ecephys+behavior.nwb"),

Checks against the files' own descriptions and the paper:

  • Counts. 15 receptive mice, as in Figures 2 and 3. The oestrogen-injected cohort has the paper's 6 mice but 42 trials, where Figure 5k has 50. The natural-cycle series has 7 mice where the paper has 4, and the male-inhibition experiment has 8 where Figure 4d has 4; which ones the paper used is not recorded. Female behaviour is annotated in 70 sessions (69 distinct trials from 23 mice, below), where Figure 1 has 74 trials from 28 mice.
  • Rates. The traces are at 10 Hz, as the files and Methods say; every timestamp step is 0.1 s. Every annotation time lies on the 30-Hz grid the descriptions give.
  • Trace types. The receptive, primed and male-inhibition files store raw Fluorescence; the 3-day natural-cycle and ovariectomy series and the 7-day oestrogen-injected series store DfOverF, described as z-scored (table above).
  • Units of the raw traces. The 33 Fluorescence series are described as raw fluorescence in lumens. Their values run from about -5,500 to 8,100, with negative values and per-cell means from 2 to 1,400, which is not a light flux; they are consistent with CNMF-E traces in arbitrary units. They are only z-scored here, so the unit does not matter to the analysis.
  • The z-scored traces. The 72 DfOverF series are described as z-scored, but per-cell means run from -1.6 to 2.4 and SDs from 0.1 to 1.8. This is consistent with the Methods, which z-score the concatenated days of a longitudinal series and then split them, though the files do not say so. They are used as stored where the analysis compares days, and z-scored again where it does not.
  • Imaging metadata. Every session file says the device is a two-photon microscope with 920-nm excitation; the Methods describe a one-photon miniscope (Inscopix nVista). Experimenter, lab and institution are placeholders, the session start time is the date the file was written, the image masks are 1 by 1 pixel so there are no cell footprints, and the file names say ecephys for imaging data. The per-mouse files describe their session as a resident-intruder assay.
  • Annotations. Male entry falls 123 to 233 s after the start of imaging, consistent with the 2-min baseline of the Methods. In 17 sessions imaging runs more than a minute past the last annotation, by up to 7 minutes; what that period holds is not described. The labels other and eat are not described in the Methods, the male channel of two m551 sessions holds sniff, and one of them grooming, the female channel of one session holds intromission, and the male-inhibition epochs are labelled laser_on in four sessions and mating_inhibition in the other four. Female annotations barely overlap (23 s summed over all sessions), so their durations can be added.
  • Subjects. One mouse is labelled 543 in its natural-cycle files and m543 in its receptive session.

Duplicated recordings and the per-mouse files¶

Some sessions have the same number of frames and cells as sessions filed under another experiment. The cell below compares their traces, cell by cell after z-scoring, and their annotations. It then matches the traces of the two per-mouse files, which carry the authors' rSLDS weights, to the natural-cycle sessions, and lists everything the per-mouse files hold under analysis and processing.

In [5]:
def match(a, b):
    """Median over cells of the best correlation of each cell of a with any cell of b."""
    n = min(len(a), len(b))
    za, zb = stats.zscore(a[:n], axis=0), stats.zscore(b[:n], axis=0)
    return np.median(np.max(za.T @ zb / n, axis=1))

for p, q in duplicate_pairs:
    a, b = data[p], data[q]
    same_shape = a.traces.shape == b.traces.shape
    r = np.median([np.corrcoef(a.traces[:, i], b.traces[:, i])[0, 1] for i in range(a.n_cells)]) if same_shape else np.nan
    ca = a.behaviour[a.behaviour.channel == "Ch1"].behavior.value_counts().to_dict()
    cb = b.behaviour[b.behaviour.channel == "Ch1"].behavior.value_counts().to_dict()
    print(f"{p.split('_ecephys')[0]} ({a.kind}) and {q.split('_ecephys')[0]} ({b.kind}): shape {a.traces.shape} / {b.traces.shape}; "
          f"median correlation of cell i with cell i {r:.4f}; male annotations identical {ca == cb}")
print()
for s, w in weights.items():
    print(f"per-mouse file sub-{s}: subject_id '{w['subject_id']}', traces {w['traces'].shape}, weight columns {w['columns']}, "
          f"session_description '{w['session_description']}', comments '{w['comments']}'")
    print(f"    its traces: per-cell mean {w['traces'].mean(0).min():.2f} to {w['traces'].mean(0).max():.2f}, "
          f"SD {w['traces'].std(0).min():.2f} to {w['traces'].std(0).max():.2f}")
    for p in cycle_paths:
        d = data[p]
        if d.traces.shape[1] == w["traces"].shape[1]:
            print(f"    {p.split('_ecephys')[0]}: {d.traces.shape}, best-match correlation {match(w['traces'], d.traces):.2f}")
        else:
            print(f"    {p.split('_ecephys')[0]}: {d.traces.shape}, cell counts differ")
m542_days = sessions_t[(sessions_t.subject == "m542") & sessions_t.experiment.str.startswith("natural")]
print(f"    the natural-cycle sessions of m542 have {sorted(set(m542_days.n_cells))} cells")
print()

Are the weights in the same cell order as the session files?¶

The weights are applied below to the stored traces of each natural-cycle day, which assumes that row i of a per-mouse weight table is column i of the session file. For each per-mouse file and the day whose traces it matches, the cell below gives the share of cells whose best-matching cell in the session file has the same index, the correlation of cell i with cell i, and whether a time shift raises it. It then tests whether the per-mouse traces are a smoothed version of the stored ones, and compares the projections onto each weight vector computed from the two sets of traces.

In [6]:
order_files = {"m541": "sub-m541_ses-WT_3d_mating_d3_ecephys+behavior.nwb",
               "m542": "sub-543_ses-WT_3d_mating_d1_ecephys+behavior.nwb"}
for s, p in order_files.items():
    A, B = weights[s]["traces"], data[p].traces
    n = min(len(A), len(B))
    za, zb = stats.zscore(A[:n], axis=0), stats.zscore(B[:n], axis=0)
    corr = za.T @ zb / n
    same = np.diag(corr)
    print(f"sub-{s} against {p.split('_ecephys')[0]} ({A.shape} and {B.shape}):")
    print(f"  best match of cell i is cell i for {(corr.argmax(1) == np.arange(len(corr))).sum()} of {len(corr)} cells; "
          f"correlation of cell i with cell i: median {np.median(same):.3f}, range {same.min():.2f} to {same.max():.2f}")
    by_shift = {}
    for lag in (-20, -10, -5, -2, 0, 2, 5, 10, 20):
        x, y = (A[lag:n], B[:n - lag]) if lag >= 0 else (A[:n + lag], B[-lag:n])
        by_shift[lag] = round(float(np.median([np.corrcoef(x[:, i], y[:, i])[0, 1] for i in range(A.shape[1])])), 3)
    print(f"  median same-index correlation by shift of the per-mouse traces (frames): {by_shift}")
    sm = {k: round(float(np.median([np.corrcoef(A[:, i], vmhvl.smooth(B, k)[:, i])[0, 1] for i in range(A.shape[1])])), 3)
          for k in (3, 9, 21, 31)}
    print(f"  the same after smoothing the stored traces with a moving average of k frames: {sm}")
    W = weights[s]["weights"]
    for k in range(W.shape[1]):
        pa, pb = A @ W[:, k], B @ W[:, k]
        print(f"  factor {k + 1}: correlation of the projection from the per-mouse traces with that from the stored traces "
              f"{np.corrcoef(pa, pb)[0, 1]:.3f}; ACHW up to 300 s {vmhvl.achw(pa[:, None], max_lag=3000)[0]:.1f} s "
              f"and {vmhvl.achw(pb[:, None], max_lag=3000)[0]:.1f} s")

The weights are in the order of the session files: 171 of 176 cells in m541 and 71 of 72 in mouse 543 best match the session cell of the same index. Cell i correlates with cell i at a median of 0.86 and 0.80, at zero shift, and the correlation rises to 0.93 and 0.90 when the stored traces are smoothed over 31 frames, so the per-mouse traces were processed differently (smoothed or denoised, and z-scored per session). The projections onto each factor from the two sets of traces correlate at 0.94 to 0.96, and the factor with the longer ACHW is the same either way. The per-mouse files hold the weight table, one trace series and the annotations; there are no latent time series or dynamics matrices.

Which natural-cycle day is the receptive one¶

The files do not say which day of the natural-cycle series was receptive, and the female's behaviour is not annotated on those days, so the paper's definition (the female shows accepting behaviour) cannot be applied. Each mouse's receptive session is also deposited separately (wt_proestrus_receptive_mating). The day whose male annotations and traces match that session is taken as the receptive day.

In [7]:
def male_onsets(s):
    b = s.behaviour
    return np.sort(b[(b.channel == "Ch1") & b.behavior.isin(vmhvl.MALE_SELF)].start.to_numpy())

receptive_day = {}
cycle = sessions_t[sessions_t.experiment == "natural cycle (3 days)"]
for subject, g in cycle.groupby("subject"):
    rec = sessions_t[(sessions_t.experiment == "receptive") & (sessions_t.subject.str.lstrip("m") == subject.lstrip("m"))]
    if rec.empty:
        print(f"{subject}: no receptive session deposited")
        continue
    r = annotations[rec.path.iloc[0]]
    for _, row in g.sort_values("day").iterrows():
        d = annotations[row.path]
        a, b = male_onsets(d), male_onsets(r)
        same_n = len(a) == len(b)
        offset = np.median(b - a) if same_n else np.nan
        spread = np.ptp(b - a) if same_n else np.nan
        line = f"{subject} day {row.day}: {len(a)} male annotations against {len(b)}"
        if same_n:
            line += f", offset {offset:.2f} s (range {spread:.2f} s)"
        if row.path in data and rec.path.iloc[0] in data:
            line += f", trace best-match correlation {match(data[row.path].traces, data[rec.path.iloc[0]].traces):.2f}"
        print(line)
        if same_n and spread < 0.5:
            receptive_day[subject] = row.day
print("receptive day by matching:", receptive_day)

Do the traces and the annotations share a clock?¶

For every session whose traces are used, a decoder predicts male contact (male sniff, mount or intromission) from 1-s bins of population activity during the interaction, with the labels shifted against the traces. If both share a clock, accuracy should be highest near zero shift, or a second or two later given the calcium indicator, and fall off at shifts of half a minute or more.

In [8]:
rng_clock = np.random.default_rng(1097_00)
shifts = [-60, -30, -10, -3, 0, 3, 10, 30, 60]
clock = []
for p in receptive_paths + oestrogen_paths + cycle_paths:
    s = data[p]
    t0, t1 = s.interaction()
    i0, i1 = int(round(t0 * vmhvl.RATE)), min(int(round(t1 * vmhvl.RATE)), s.n_frames)
    y = vmhvl.bin_frames(vmhvl.zscore(s.traces)[i0:i1], 10)
    lab = vmhvl.bin_frames(vmhvl.raster(s.behaviour, vmhvl.MALE_SELF, s.n_frames, "Ch1")[i0:i1].astype(float), 10) >= 0.5
    acc = vmhvl.shifted_decoding(y, lab, shifts, rng_clock)
    clock.append({"session": p.split("_ecephys")[0], "positives": int(lab.sum()), "bins": len(lab), **dict(zip(shifts, acc))})
clock = pd.DataFrame(clock).set_index("session")
best = clock[shifts].idxmax(axis=1)
near = clock[[-3, 0, 3]].max(axis=1)
far = clock[[-60, 60]].max(axis=1)
print(f"{len(clock)} sessions. Shift of best accuracy: {best.value_counts().sort_index().to_dict()}")
print(f"best accuracy within 3 s of zero: median {near.median():.2f} (range {near.min():.2f} to {near.max():.2f}); "
      f"best at +-60 s: median {far.median():.2f}")
clock_fail = clock.index[(near - far) < 0.05].tolist()
print(f"sessions where accuracy near zero exceeds that at +-60 s by less than 0.05: {', '.join(clock_fail) or 'none'}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
for _, r in clock.iterrows():
    ax.plot(shifts, r[shifts].to_numpy(), color="0.6", lw=0.7)
ax.plot(shifts, clock[shifts].median(), color="k", lw=2, label="median")
ax.set_xlabel("shift of the labels (s)"); ax.set_ylabel("balanced accuracy"); ax.axhline(0.5, ls="--", color="k", lw=0.8)
ax.legend(frameon=False); plt.tight_layout()
print(f"plotted accuracies range from {clock[shifts].min().min():.2f} to {clock[shifts].max().max():.2f}")

Accuracy is highest within 3 s of zero shift in 62 of the 63 sessions. Two oestrogen-injected sessions, m928 day 2 and m940 day 7, gain less than 0.05 over the shifts of 60 s, so a shared clock is not established for them. They stay in the behaviour claims, which use only the annotations; Extended Data Figure 10c is also shown without them.

Trial sets for the behaviour claims¶

The paper's Figure 1 uses 74 trials from 28 mice without listing them. The dandiset has female annotations for 70 sessions; one of them (m764 natural-cycle day 1) is the same recording as m764's primed session, so 69 distinct trials remain. Two sets are read: all of them, and the receptive ones (any lordosis or wiggle). For the interbout interval, which needs only the male's annotations, a third set adds every other distinct session outside the male-inhibition experiment. A day of a 3-day or 7-day series is not distinct when it was matched above to a separately deposited session of the same mouse, or has the same number of frames as one. The male annotations of the same recording can differ between its two files (m551's ovariectomy day 3 and primed session, above, have identical traces), so they are not required to match. The cell prints the evidence for each pair, m438's other days for comparison, and the closest candidates for the three mice whose 7-day series and receptive session are both deposited.

In [9]:
def length(p):
    t0, t1 = annotations[p].interaction()
    return t1 - t0


def describe(p, q):
    a, b = annotations[p], annotations[q]
    trace = f"; trace best-match correlation {match(data[p].traces, data[q].traces):.2f}" if p in data and q in data else ""
    if p in data and q in data and data[p].traces.shape == data[q].traces.shape:
        trace += (", median correlation of cell i with cell i "
                  f"{np.median([np.corrcoef(data[p].traces[:, i], data[q].traces[:, i])[0, 1] for i in range(a.n_cells)]):.3f}")
    return (f"frames {a.n_frames} / {b.n_frames}, cells {a.n_cells} / {b.n_cells}, male onsets {len(male_onsets(a))} / "
            f"{len(male_onsets(b))}, interaction {length(p):.1f} / {length(q):.1f} s{trace}")


dup_of = {}
for _, row in sessions_t[sessions_t.experiment.str.contains("days")].iterrows():
    others = sessions_t[(sessions_t.subject.str.lstrip("m") == row.subject.lstrip("m"))
                        & sessions_t.experiment.isin(["receptive", "ovariectomised, primed"])]
    for _, o in others.iterrows():
        matched = receptive_day.get(row.subject) == row.day and o.experiment == "receptive" and row.experiment.startswith("natural")
        if matched or o.n_frames == row.n_frames:
            dup_of[row.path] = o.path
print(f"{len(dup_of)} days of 3-day or 7-day series duplicate a separately deposited session:")
for p, q in dup_of.items():
    print(f"  {p.split('_ecephys')[0]} = {q.split('_ecephys')[0]}: {describe(p, q)}")
p438 = "sub-m438_ses-wt_proestrus_receptive_mating_ecephys+behavior.nwb"
print("  for comparison, m438's other natural-cycle days against its receptive session:")
for p in m438_days[1:]:
    print(f"    {p.split('_ecephys')[0]}: {describe(p, p438)}")
print("Closest 7-day session to the receptive session, by frame count, for the mice that have both:")
for subject in ("m928", "m930", "m940"):
    rec = sessions_t[(sessions_t.subject == subject) & (sessions_t.experiment == "receptive")].path.iloc[0]
    days = sessions_t[(sessions_t.subject == subject) & sessions_t.experiment.str.startswith("oestrogen")]
    for p in days.iloc[(days.n_frames - annotations[rec].n_frames).abs().argsort()[:2]].path:
        print(f"  {p.split('_ecephys')[0]} against the receptive session: {describe(p, rec)}")


def onset_alignment(p, q, tol=0.2):
    """Largest share of p's male onsets that fall within tol s of one of q's under one constant offset."""
    a, b = male_onsets(annotations[p]), male_onsets(annotations[q])
    offsets = (b[None, :] - a[:, None]).ravel()
    offsets = np.unique(np.round(offsets[np.abs(offsets) < 600], 1))
    best = max(offsets, key=lambda o: np.sum(np.min(np.abs(a[:, None] + o - b[None, :]), 1) < tol))
    return np.mean(np.min(np.abs(a[:, None] + best - b[None, :]), 1) < tol), best


def shifted_match(p, q, max_shift=100, step=5):
    """Median over cells of p of the best correlation with any cell of q, at the frame shift that maximises it."""
    x, y = data[p].traces, data[q].traces
    best = (-1.0, 0)
    for k in range(-max_shift, max_shift + 1, step):
        u, v = (x[k:], y) if k >= 0 else (x, y[-k:])
        n = min(len(u), len(v))
        zu, zv = stats.zscore(u[:n], axis=0), stats.zscore(v[:n], axis=0)
        best = max(best, (float(np.median(np.max(zu.T @ zv / n, axis=1))), k))
    return best


print("Alignment checks, not set out in advance. For each pair: the share of male onsets matched within 0.2 s under\n"
      "one constant offset, and the trace best-match correlation at the best shift of up to 10 s in 0.5-s steps.")
p930 = sessions_t[(sessions_t.subject == "m930") & (sessions_t.experiment == "receptive")].path.iloc[0]
pairs = [(p, dup_of[p]) for p in dup_of if p in data and dup_of[p] in data]
pairs += [(p, p438) for p in m438_days[1:]]
pairs += [(p, p930) for p in sessions_t[(sessions_t.subject == "m930") & sessions_t.experiment.str.startswith("oestrogen")]
          .sort_values("day").path]
for p, q in pairs:
    share, offset = onset_alignment(p, q)
    r, k = shifted_match(p, q) if p in data and q in data else (np.nan, 0)
    print(f"  {p.split('_ecephys')[0]} against {q.split('_ecephys')[0]}: onsets matched {share:.2f} (offset {offset:.1f} s); "
          f"best-match correlation {r:.2f} at shift {k / vmhvl.RATE:+.1f} s")

distinct = sessions_t[~sessions_t.path.isin(dup_of)]
trial_sets = {
    "all annotated": distinct[distinct.female_annotated].path.tolist(),
    "receptive": distinct[distinct.female_annotated & distinct.receptive].path.tolist(),
    "all distinct, male annotation": distinct[distinct.experiment != "male inhibition"].path.tolist(),
}
for name, ps in trial_sets.items():
    subj = sessions_t.set_index("path").loc[ps, "subject"].str.lstrip("m")
    print(f"{name}: {len(ps)} trials from {subj.nunique()} mice")


def clipped(iv, t0, t1):
    return np.clip(iv, t0, t1)


def duration(s, labels, channel):
    t0, t1 = s.interaction()
    iv = clipped(vmhvl.intervals(s.behaviour, labels, channel), t0, t1)
    return float((iv[:, 1] - iv[:, 0]).sum())

Figure 1b: accepting behaviour escalates over the interaction¶

During mating the probability of accepting behaviours (lordosis, wiggle) increases gradually over the interaction, while resistance behaviours (dart, top up, kick, turn) first increase and then slowly decrease.

In [10]:
BIN, SPAN = 20, 600
n_bins = SPAN // BIN


def group_curves(paths, labels):
    out = np.full((len(paths), n_bins), np.nan)
    for i, p in enumerate(paths):
        s = annotations[p]
        t0, t1 = s.interaction()
        frames = int(np.ceil(t1 * vmhvl.RATE)) + 1
        r = vmhvl.raster(s.behaviour, labels, frames, "Ch2")
        for k in range(n_bins):
            a, b = t0 + k * BIN, t0 + (k + 1) * BIN
            if b <= t1:
                out[i, k] = r[int(round(a * vmhvl.RATE)):int(round(b * vmhvl.RATE))].mean()
    return out


def judge_escalation(acc, res):
    counts = np.sum(~np.isnan(acc), 0)
    keep = counts >= 5
    ma, mr = np.nanmean(acc, 0)[keep], np.nanmean(res, 0)[keep]
    k = len(ma)
    rho, p = stats.spearmanr(np.arange(k), ma)
    third = k // 3
    first, last = ma[:third].mean(), ma[-third:].mean()
    run = np.convolve(mr, np.ones(3) / 3, "same")
    run[0], run[-1] = mr[:2].mean(), mr[-2:].mean()
    peak = int(np.argmax(run))
    accept_ok = rho > 0 and p < 0.05 and last > first
    resist_ok = 0 < peak < 2 * k / 3 and mr[-third:].mean() < run[peak]
    return dict(bins_kept=k, accept_spearman=round(rho, 2), accept_p=p, accept_first_third=round(first, 3),
                accept_last_third=round(last, 3), resist_peak_bin=peak, resist_peak=round(run[peak], 3),
                resist_first_bin=round(mr[0], 3), resist_last_third=round(mr[-third:].mean(), 3),
                accepting_escalates=accept_ok, resistance_rises_then_falls=resist_ok), ma, mr, keep


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4), sharey=True)
rows = {}
for ax, name in zip(axes, ["all annotated", "receptive"]):
    ps = trial_sets[name]
    acc, res, app = (group_curves(ps, g) for g in (vmhvl.ACCEPT, vmhvl.RESIST, vmhvl.APPETITIVE))
    verdict, ma, mr, keep = judge_escalation(acc, res)
    rows[name] = verdict
    t = (np.arange(n_bins)[keep] + 0.5) * BIN
    for curve, label, color in ((acc, "accept", "C3"), (res, "resistance", "C0"), (app, "appetitive", "C2")):
        m = np.nanmean(curve, 0)[keep]
        se = np.nanstd(curve, 0)[keep] / np.sqrt(np.sum(~np.isnan(curve), 0)[keep])
        ax.plot(t, m, color=color, label=label); ax.fill_between(t, m - se, m + se, color=color, alpha=0.2)
    ax.set_title(f"{name} ({len(ps)} trials)", fontsize=10); ax.set_xlabel("time from male entry (s)")
    print(f"{name}: trials in each kept bin {np.sum(~np.isnan(acc), 0)[keep].tolist()}")
    print(f"{name}: trials per bin from {np.sum(~np.isnan(acc), 0)[keep].min()} to {np.sum(~np.isnan(acc), 0)[keep].max()}; "
          f"plotted means range {min(np.nanmean(c, 0)[keep].min() for c in (acc, res, app)):.3f} to "

Then, because later bins hold only the longer trials, two checks not named in the criterion: the same correlation within each trial, over the bins that trial covers, and the mean curve over the first 300 s (15 bins) using only the trials that cover all of them.

Result: reproduced. Over the first 600 s after male entry, the mean probability of accepting behaviour rises with time (Spearman 0.74, p = 3e-6, on all 69 annotated trials; 0.59, p = 6e-4, on the 58 receptive trials), from 0.11 in the first third of the bins to 0.19 in the last. Resistance peaks in the third bin and falls to 0.07 in the last third, under both sets. Later bins hold fewer trials (69 in the first bins, 11 in the last), but with the same 63 trials in each of the first 15 bins the rise remains (Spearman 0.63, p = 0.012; 0.080 to 0.151). It is a property of the pooled trials: within single mice the correlation is positive in 12 of 23, and within single trials in 33 of 58 (median Spearman 0.01, sign test p = 0.36).

Figure 1c: most female mating behaviour responds to the male¶

Females spend 83.9% of their mating behaviour time in male-responsive behaviours (accepting, resistance, staying) and 16.1% in self-initiated ones (approach, sniff, check genital area).

def behaviour_times(paths):
    rows = []
    for p in paths:
        s = annotations[p]
        t0, t1 = s.interaction()
        rows.append(dict(path=p, subject=sessions_t.set_index("path").subject[p].lstrip("m"),
                         interaction=t1 - t0,
                         responsive=duration(s, vmhvl.RESPONSIVE, "Ch2"),
                         female_self=duration(s, vmhvl.FEMALE_SELF, "Ch2"),
                         male_self=duration(s, vmhvl.MALE_SELF, "Ch1"),
                         accept=duration(s, vmhvl.ACCEPT, "Ch2")))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

def copulation(p, gap):
    s = annotations[p]
    return vmhvl.bouts(vmhvl.intervals(s.behaviour, vmhvl.COPULATION, "Ch1"), gap)

        b = [copulation(p, gap) for p in ps]
        ibi = np.concatenate([x[1:, 0] - x[:-1, 1] for x in b if len(x) > 1])
        dur = np.concatenate([x[:, 1] - x[:, 0] for x in b])
        rows.append({"trials": name, "merge gaps up to": gap_name, "trials n": len(ps),
                     "bouts": len(dur), "intervals": len(ibi), "mean interval (s)": round(ibi.mean(), 2),
                     "median interval (s)": round(np.median(ibi), 2), "mean bout (s)": round(dur.mean(), 2),

Result: reproduced. With mount and intromission annotations less than 0.1 s apart merged into bouts, the mean interbout interval is 14.0 s over the 69 annotated trials, 14.9 s over receptive trials and 14.6 s over all 88 distinct sessions, against 13.7 s in the paper. Merging gaps up to 1 s lengthens it to 15.5 to 16.3 s, and not merging at all shortens it to 9.8 to 10.8 s; the paper's figure matches the near-contiguous merging. The 69 trials give 1,540 bouts and 1,471 intervals.

Figure 1g: females stay social during bouts and after them¶

Females show social behaviours (accepting, resistance and appetitive) for 62% of the duration of each male copulation bout and continue them for 23% of each interbout interval.

In [18]:
def social_fractions(ps, gap=0.1):
    in_bout, in_ibi, tb, sb, ti, si = [], [], 0, 0, 0, 0
    for p in ps:
        s = annotations[p]
        frames = int(np.ceil(s.behaviour.stop.max() * vmhvl.RATE)) + 2
        social = vmhvl.raster(s.behaviour, vmhvl.SOCIAL, frames, "Ch2")
        b = copulation(p, gap)
        for (a, z) in b:
            seg = social[int(round(a * vmhvl.RATE)):max(int(round(z * vmhvl.RATE)), int(round(a * vmhvl.RATE)) + 1)]
            in_bout.append(seg.mean()); tb += len(seg); sb += seg.sum()
        for (a, z) in zip(b[:-1, 1], b[1:, 0]):
            seg = social[int(round(a * vmhvl.RATE)):int(round(z * vmhvl.RATE))]
            if len(seg):
                in_ibi.append(seg.mean()); ti += len(seg); si += seg.sum()
    return np.array(in_bout), np.array(in_ibi), sb / tb, si / ti

rows = []
for name in ("all annotated", "receptive"):
    fb, fi, pb, pi = social_fractions(trial_sets[name])
    rows.append({"trials": name, "bouts": len(fb), "intervals": len(fi),
                 "bout, mean of fractions": round(fb.mean(), 3), "bout, pooled": round(pb, 3),
                 "interval, mean of fractions": round(fi.mean(), 3), "interval, pooled": round(pi, 3)})

This is the only one of the four readings that matches: over receptive trials the interval value is 17.4%, and pooled over time, not averaged over bouts, the values are 74% and 11%.

Variant, not set out in advance: the readings that match for Figures 1c, 1d, 1e and 1g, without m930's oestrogen days 3 and 4, the two days closest to m930's receptive session in frame count and trace match in the checks above.

Figure 2c: few cells are tuned to any one behaviour¶

Only a small percentage of VMHvl alpha-cells (approximately 2 to 13%) are tuned to any one mating behaviour by choice probability; most show mixed selectivity.

In the 15 receptive sessions, each cell's z-scored trace is averaged in 1-s bins over the interaction. A bin belongs to a behaviour when the behaviour covers at least half of it.

In [20]:
rng_cp = np.random.default_rng(1097_02)
cp_behaviours = [(b, "Ch2") for b in vmhvl.FEMALE_MATING] + [(b, "Ch1") for b in vmhvl.MALE_SELF]
cp_rows = []
for p in receptive_paths:
    s = data[p]
    t0, t1 = s.interaction()
    i0, i1 = int(round(t0 * vmhvl.RATE)), min(int(round(t1 * vmhvl.RATE)), s.n_frames)
    y = vmhvl.bin_frames(vmhvl.zscore(s.traces)[i0:i1], 10)
    for b, ch in cp_behaviours:
        lab = vmhvl.bin_frames(vmhvl.raster(s.behaviour, [b], s.n_frames, ch)[i0:i1].astype(float), 10) >= 0.5
        if lab.sum() < 10 or (~lab).sum() < 10:
            continue
        cp, mu, sd = vmhvl.choice_probability(y, lab, rng_cp)
        tuned = ((cp > 0.7) | (cp < 0.3)) & (np.abs(cp - mu) > 2 * sd)
        cp_rows.append(dict(subject=s.subject, behaviour=b, bins=int(lab.sum()), cells=s.n_cells,
                            tuned=int(tuned.sum()), tuned_up=int((tuned & (cp > 0.5)).sum()),
                            beyond_2sd_only=int((np.abs(cp - mu) > 2 * sd).sum())))

Variant, not named in the criterion: choice probability between pairs of behaviours, as the Methods describe it ("for any behaviour pair"). rng_cp_pairs = np.random.default_rng(1097_06)
pair_rows = []
for p in receptive_paths:
    s = data[p]
    t0, t1 = s.interaction()
    i0, i1 = int(round(t0 * vmhvl.RATE)), min(int(round(t1 * vmhvl.RATE)), s.n_frames)
    y = vmhvl.bin_frames(vmhvl.zscore(s.traces)[i0:i1], 10)
    for group, channel, names in (("female", "Ch2", vmhvl.FEMALE_MATING), ("male", "Ch1", vmhvl.MALE_SELF)):
        labs = {b: vmhvl.bin_frames(vmhvl.raster(s.behaviour, [b], s.n_frames, channel)[i0:i1].astype(float), 10) >= 0.5
                for b in names}
        for i, a in enumerate(names):
            for b in names[i + 1:]:
                la, lb = labs[a] & ~labs[b], labs[b] & ~labs[a]
                if la.sum() < 10 or lb.sum() < 10:
                    continue
                keep = la | lb
                cp, mu, sd = vmhvl.choice_probability(y[keep], la[keep], rng_cp_pairs)
                tuned = ((cp > 0.7) | (cp < 0.3)) & (np.abs(cp - mu) > 2 * sd)
                pair_rows.append(dict(subject=s.subject, group=group, pair=f"{a} vs {b}", cells=s.n_cells, tuned=int(tuned.sum())))

Result: not reproduced. With the procedure set out in the criterion, 6.9% (approach) to 37.4% (dart) of cells are tuned to a behaviour, with a median over the 11 behaviours analysed of 22.0%, against about 2 to 13% in the paper. Eight of the 11 exceed 15%. Comparing pairs of behaviours, as the Methods describe, tunes more cells, not fewer: 15.4% to 57.6% over 20 pairs (median 39.3%), and no pair falls within 1 to 15%. The shuffle criterion alone (beyond 2 SD of shuffled labels) passes 21% to 75% of cells; it permutes bins without regard to the slow changes in the traces, as the paper's does, so it removes few.

Figure 2e and 2f: behaviour explains little of a cell's activity; other cells explain more¶

A linear model of each neuron's activity from behaviour explains little of its variance, with mean cross-validated R2 of 0.08 from female behaviours, 0.14 from male behaviours and 0.15 from both.

Adding the activity of the other simultaneously imaged neurons as regressors raises the mean cross-validated R2 to 0.46.

Ridge regression of each z-scored trace, over the interaction, on the behaviour rasters delayed by 0 to 10 s in 1-s steps; tenfold contiguous cross-validation.

In [23]:
lags = np.arange(0, 101, 10)
rng_glm = np.random.default_rng(1097_03)


def glm_designs(s):
    t0, t1 = s.interaction()
    i0, i1 = int(round(t0 * vmhvl.RATE)), min(int(round(t1 * vmhvl.RATE)), s.n_frames)
    Y = vmhvl.zscore(s.traces)[i0:i1]
    fem = np.column_stack([vmhvl.raster(s.behaviour, [b], s.n_frames, "Ch2")[i0:i1] for b in vmhvl.FEMALE_MATING])
    mal = np.column_stack([vmhvl.raster(s.behaviour, [b], s.n_frames, "Ch1")[i0:i1] for b in vmhvl.MALE_SELF])
    Xf, Xm = vmhvl.lagged(fem.astype(float), lags), vmhvl.lagged(mal.astype(float), lags)
    Xb = np.hstack([Xf, Xm])
    return Y, {"female": (Xf, None), "male": (Xm, None), "both": (Xb, None),
               "coupling": (np.hstack([Xb, Y]), Xb.shape[1] + np.arange(Y.shape[1]))}


glm, glm_random = [], []
for p in receptive_paths:
    s = data[p]
    Y, designs = glm_designs(s)
    for rng, out in ((None, glm), (rng_glm, glm_random)):
        r2 = {}
        for name, (X, exclude) in designs.items():
            r2[name], pred, fold_of = vmhvl.cv_ridge(X, Y, exclude=exclude, rng=rng, return_pred=True)
            r2[f"{name}, within folds"] = vmhvl.within_fold_r2(Y, pred, fold_of)
        pred = vmhvl.intercept_predictions(Y, fold_of)
        r2["intercept only"] = vmhvl.pooled_r2(Y, pred)
        r2["intercept only, within folds"] = vmhvl.within_fold_r2(Y, pred, fold_of)
        for i in range(Y.shape[1]):
            out.append(dict(subject=s.subject, cell=i, **{k: v[i] for k, v in r2.items()}))
glm, glm_random = pd.DataFrame(glm), pd.DataFrame(glm_random)
models = ["female", "male", "both", "coupling"]
expected = {"female": 0.08, "male": 0.14, "both": 0.15, "coupling": 0.46}
summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "expected": expected,
    "mean over cells": glm[models].mean(),
    "mean of mouse means": glm.groupby("subject")[models].mean().mean(),
    "median over cells": glm[models].median(),
    "cells below 0": (glm[models] < 0).sum(),
    "variant, random folds, mean over cells": glm_random[models].mean(),
    "variant, random folds, mean of mouse means": glm_random.groupby("subject")[models].mean().mean(),
}).round(3)
print(f"{len(glm)} cells from {glm.subject.nunique()} mice; cvR2 range over cells: "
      + "; ".join(f"{m} {glm[m].min():.2f} to {glm[m].max():.2f}" for m in models))
summary

The baseline for these numbers: a model with only an intercept, predicting each held-out fold by the mean of the training frames, scored under the same folds. The difference between a model and this baseline is what behaviour (or coupling) adds. R2 is also computed within each held-out fold, against that fold's own mean, and averaged over folds; this removes the offset between folds but gives a fold of 10% of the interaction to each score.

Result: partially reproduced. With contiguous folds and the penalty chosen by cross-validation within each training set, the mean cross-validated R2 is -0.041 from female behaviours, -0.005 from male behaviours and -0.004 from both (means of mouse means -0.026, 0.014 and 0.016), against 0.08, 0.14 and 0.15. The ordering holds, both against male by a margin of only 0.0003 (0.0014 over mouse means), and all three are below 0.25. With the penalty chosen on the last fifth of each training set, the design first used, the values are -0.077, -0.013 and -0.057 and both scores below male, so the ordering failure came from that selection; the outcome is judged on the cross-validated penalty, a variant not set out in advance. A model with only an intercept scores -0.086 under these folds, because the mean of a held-out block of time differs from the mean of the rest. The gain over it is 0.045, 0.081 and 0.082 (mouse means 0.054, 0.095 and 0.096), below the paper's values. Within single folds, with the last-fifth penalty, R2 is dominated by the same offsets (median -0.61 to -0.71 against -0.70 for the intercept). With frames assigned to folds at random the means are 0.229, 0.207 and 0.322, with neighbouring frames in both training and test sets; the value from both behaviours is then above 0.25. This test is weak: no design run here separates what behaviour explains from the slow drift of the traces.

Result: reproduced. Adding the instantaneous activity of the other cells raises the mean cross-validated R2 to 0.477 over cells (0.458 over mouse means) with the cross-validated penalty, and 0.450 (0.434) with the last-fifth penalty, against 0.46 in the paper. With the last-fifth penalty 73 of 1,335 cells remain below zero, and the gain over the intercept-only baseline is 0.536 (0.563 with the cross-validated penalty). With random folds the value is 0.814. It shares the fold design of Figure 2e.

Figure 2i: many cells are persistent¶

About 30% of cells have an autocorrelation half-width (ACHW) longer than 25 s, and the mean ACHW is 20 s, longer than the mean interbout interval.

The criterion's readings are the whole recording and the interaction. In 7 of the 15 sessions the whole recording includes several minutes of imaging after the last annotation, so a third window, not named in the criterion, runs from the start of imaging to the end of the annotation.

In [28]:
achw_rows = []
for p in receptive_paths:
    s = data[p]
    t0, t1 = s.interaction()
    i0, i1 = int(round(t0 * vmhvl.RATE)), min(int(round(t1 * vmhvl.RATE)), s.n_frames)
    windows = (("whole recording", (0, s.n_frames)), ("interaction", (i0, i1)),
               ("variant, start of imaging to end of annotation", (0, i1)))
    for window, (a, b) in windows:
        for smoothed in (True, False):
            y = vmhvl.prepare(s.traces[a:b], smoothed=smoothed)
            for first in (False, True):
                h = vmhvl.achw(y, first_crossing=first)
                achw_rows.append(dict(subject=s.subject, window=window, smoothed=smoothed,
                                      rule="first crossing" if first else "closest to 0.5 (code)",
                                      cells=len(h), above_25=(h > 25).sum(), sum=h.sum(), at_cap=(h >= 50).sum()))

Result: not reproduced. Over the whole recording, smoothed as in the authors' code, 20.0% of cells have an ACHW above 25 s and the mean ACHW is 15.5 s, against 30% and 20 s. Every other reading gives the same or less: the first-crossing rule 19.9% and 15.5 s, the others 10 to 17% and 9.9 to 13.1 s. Ending the window at the last annotation, which drops the unannotated imaging at the end of 7 sessions, gives 15.5 to 19.7% and 12.7 to 15.0 s. The mouse-level fractions range from 0 to 0.48, and four mice (m540, m551, m930, m940) reach 0.28 or more; Figure 2i's lower panel has n = 4 mice, so the paper's 30% may come from a subset, which the paper does not identify. The mean ACHW of 15.5 s is still longer than the mean interbout interval of 14.0 s found above.

Extended Data Figure 6e and Figure 5h: the receptive-day dimension on unreceptive days¶

Projected onto the integration dimension found on the receptive day, activity on unreceptive days does not ramp and stays low during male mounting (normalised value 0.09 on unreceptive against 0.69 on receptive days, n = 4 mice).

The authors' rSLDS weights are deposited for two mice: in sub-m541/sub-m541_behavior.nwb, whose cells are those of m541's natural-cycle days, and in sub-m542/sub-m542_behavior.nwb, whose cells are those of mouse 543 (shown in the data check). The receptive days are m541 day 3 and 543 day 1, matched above.

In [30]:
cycle_mice = {"m541": ("m541", "sub-m541_ses-WT_3d_mating_d{}_ecephys+behavior.nwb"),
              "543": ("m542", "sub-543_ses-WT_3d_mating_d{}_ecephys+behavior.nwb")}
proj = {}
for mouse, (wfile, pattern) in cycle_mice.items():
    rday = int(receptive_day[mouse])
    days = {d: data[pattern.format(d)] for d in (1, 2, 3)}
    W = weights[wfile]["weights"]
    rec = days[rday]
    t_entry = int(round(rec.interaction()[0] * vmhvl.RATE))
    capped = [vmhvl.achw((rec.traces @ W[:, k])[:, None])[0] for k in range(W.shape[1])]
    # The 500-lag cap of the authors' ACHW can tie; the factor is chosen with lags up to 300 s.
    halfwidths = [vmhvl.achw((rec.traces @ W[:, k])[:, None], max_lag=3000)[0] for k in range(W.shape[1])]
    chosen = int(np.argmax(halfwidths))
    print(f"mouse {mouse} (weights from sub-{wfile}): ACHW of the receptive-day projection, capped at 50 s, "
          f"factor 1 {capped[0]:.1f} s and factor 2 {capped[1]:.1f} s; up to 300 s, {halfwidths[0]:.1f} s and "
          f"{halfwidths[1]:.1f} s; integration factor {chosen + 1}")
    for k in (chosen, 1 - chosen):
        x_rec = rec.traces @ W[:, k]
        sign = 1 if x_rec[t_entry:].mean() > x_rec[:t_entry].mean() else -1
        w = sign * W[:, k]
        xs = {d: s.traces @ w for d, s in days.items()}
        lo, hi = min(x.min() for x in xs.values()), max(x.max() for x in xs.values())
        rlo, rhi = xs[rday].min(), xs[rday].max()
        rows = []
        for d, s in days.items():
            mount = vmhvl.raster(s.behaviour, ["mount"], s.n_frames, "Ch1")
            t0, t1 = s.interaction()
            e = int(round(t0 * vmhvl.RATE))
            end = min(int(round(t1 * vmhvl.RATE)), s.n_frames)
            x = xs[d]
            rows.append({"day": d, "receptive": d == rday, "mount frames": int(mount.sum()),
                         "intromission bouts": int((s.behaviour.behavior == "intromission").sum()),
                         "mounting, min-max over 3 days": round(((x[mount] - lo) / (hi - lo)).mean(), 3),
                         "mounting, receptive-day range": round(((x[mount] - rlo) / (rhi - rlo)).mean(), 3),
                         "ramp: last 100 s minus 60 s before entry (SD of receptive day)":
                             round((x[end - 1000:end].mean() - x[e - 600:e].mean()) / xs[rday].std(), 2)})
        table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("day")
        if k == chosen:
            proj[mouse] = dict(factor=k + 1, sign=sign, xs=xs, rday=rday, lo=lo, hi=hi, table=table)
            print(f"  factor {k + 1} (the integration factor), sign {sign:+d}:")
        else:
            print(f"  variant, factor {k + 1}, sign {sign:+d}:")
        print(table.to_string())
    print()

for ax, (mouse, pr) in zip(axes, proj.items()):

print("all plotted values lie in 0 to 1 by construction")

all plotted values lie in 0 to 1 by construction

Result: partially reproduced. In m541, on the integration factor (factor 2, chosen by its receptive-day ACHW of 105 s against 57 s), the normalised value during mounting is 0.61 on the receptive day against 0.23 and 0.19 on the unreceptive days. The paper has 0.69 against 0.09, so the receptive-day value is close to the paper's and the unreceptive values are about twice it. In mouse 543 (factor 1, ACHW 129 s against 32 s) the value is 0.61 on the receptive day against 0.64 and 0.63, so not higher. The ramp part of the claim holds in both mice: from before male entry to the last 100 s of the interaction the projection rises by 2.5 and 2.1 receptive-day SDs on the receptive day, against 0.0 to 0.5 and -0.4 to 0.2 on the unreceptive days. The outcome depends on which factor is taken as the integration factor, which the files do not say. On the other factor the receptive day is higher in both mice (m541 factor 1, 0.62 against 0.48 and 0.49; 543 factor 2, 0.66 against 0.54 and 0.51), which would meet the criterion in both, though on 543's factor 2 the unreceptive days also ramp (1.07 and 1.03 SDs). The weights line up with the session files: the best-matching session cell is the cell of the same index for 171 of 176 and 71 of 72 cells, and the projections from the per-mouse traces and from the stored traces correlate at 0.94 to 0.96.

Extended Data Figure 7: single-cell persistence across the cycle¶

Cells weighted on the integration dimension have shorter ACHW on unreceptive than on receptive days (16.1 +- 0.8 s against 25.2 +- 1.5 s, P < 0.001), while cells that do not contribute to it do not change.

Result: partially reproduced. In both mice, cells weighted on the integration factor have longer ACHWs on the receptive day than on the unreceptive days: 28.4 against 17.2 s in m541 (KS p = 2e-5) and 26.7 against 9.1 s in 543 (KS p = 2e-4), against 25.2 and 16.1 s in the paper. The other cells do not differ in m541 (14.9 against 12.1 s, KS p = 0.23) but do in 543 (12.8 against 10.8 s, KS p = 0.005). With the top 25% of weights in place of the one-SD threshold the same pattern holds; with the top 10%, the weighted cells of 543 (8 cells) no longer differ (p = 0.13). The change is not specific to the integration factor. In m541 the 44 cells above one SD on the other factor, 23 of them shared with the integration factor, lengthen as much (30.8 against 17.5 s, KS p = 7e-6). In 543 the 20 cells of the other factor, 7 of them shared, do not differ at p 0.05 (21.0 against 12.9 s, p = 0.07).

Extended Data Figure 10c: the population mean does not track receptivity¶

In the same trials, the area under the curve of the population mean of all neurons does not correlate with the percentage of time spent in accepting behaviours.

A variant leaves out the sessions that failed the clock check above.

Result: reproduced. Over the 42 trials, the area under the population mean does not correlate with the percentage of time in accepting behaviour under any of the three readings (r2 = 0.015, 0.003 and 0.027; p = 0.45, 0.73 and 0.30). Within mice the Spearman correlations run from -0.67 to 0.52. Without the two sessions that failed the clock check, r2 is 0.011, 0.005 and 0.025 over 40 trials.

Claims that cannot be tested here¶

The cell below records what the dandiset holds for the blocked claims, so that the reasons can be checked. Two exploratory checks follow; they are not judged against the claims.

Pencil cup (Extended Data Figure 3a-c). The Methods say imaging continued for 3 to 5 minutes with the male under a pencil cup, and nothing in the files marks that period. The cell lists, for every session, how long imaging runs past the last annotation. For the receptive sessions with at least 3 minutes of it, it compares each cell's ACHW in that tail with its ACHW in the interaction, and in the last stretch of the interaction of the same length as the tail, since a shorter window alone shortens the ACHW. Whether the tail is the pencil-cup period is not known.

    h_end = vmhvl.achw(vmhvl.prepare(s.traces[max(i0, i1 - n_tail):i1]))

    rows.append({"mouse": s.subject, "tail (s)": n_tail / vmhvl.RATE, "cells": s.n_cells,

In all 7 receptive sessions with at least 3 minutes of imaging after the last annotation, the mean ACHW in that tail (4.0 to 11.5 s) is shorter than over the interaction (7.3 to 17.9 s), as the paper reports for the pencil cup. Against the stretch at the end of the interaction of the same length it is longer in 5 of the 7, and differs significantly only in m551 (Wilcoxon p below 0.001, tail longer; elsewhere p 0.11 to 0.47), so the shorter ACHW here comes from the shorter window. These 7 sessions hold 544 cells, where the paper has 470 from 5 mice. Since the files do not say what the tail holds, the claim stays blocked.

Single-cell ramps (Extended Data Figure 4a,b) in the two mice with deposited weights. The paper does not define its ideal ramp; here it is 0 before male entry and rises linearly to 1 at the end of the annotation. Each cell's smoothed, z-scored trace on the receptive day, up to the end of the annotation, is correlated with it, for the cells weighted on the integration factor (as in Extended Data Figure 7) and for the others. The paper's 56% comes from 15 receptive sessions with the dimension refitted in each.

for mouse, (wfile, pattern) in cycle_mice.items():
    pr = proj[mouse]
    s = data[pattern.format(pr["rday"])]
    t0, t1 = s.interaction()
    i0, i1 = int(round(t0 * vmhvl.RATE)), min(int(round(t1 * vmhvl.RATE)), s.n_frames)
    w = weights[wfile]["weights"][:, pr["factor"] - 1]
    weighted = np.abs(w) > np.std(w, ddof=1)
    y = vmhvl.prepare(s.traces)[:i1]
    ramp = np.zeros(i1)
    ramp[i0:] = np.linspace(0, 1, i1 - i0)
    r = np.array([np.corrcoef(y[:, i], ramp)[0, 1] for i in range(y.shape[1])])
    for group, m in (("weighted", weighted), ("other", ~weighted)):
        print(f"mouse {mouse}, {group} cells ({m.sum()}): r2 above 0.5 in {(r[m] ** 2 > 0.5).sum()} "
              f"({(r[m] ** 2 > 0.5).mean():.0%}); r from {r[m].min():.2f} to {r[m].max():.2f}, median {np.median(r[m]):.2f}")

With this ramp, 0 of 44 weighted cells in m541 and 1 of 14 in mouse 543 have r2 above 0.5, against 56% in the paper. The ramp is a choice here and the mice are 2 natural-cycle mice, not the 15 receptive ones, so this is not a test of the claim, which stays blocked.

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.

How this differs from the paper's analysis¶

  • No rSLDS model is fitted, so the paper's central claims about the line attractor are not tested directly. The two tested claims about it use the authors' deposited weights for two mice where the paper has four, and choose the integration factor by its autocorrelation, since the files do not say which factor it is. Both outcomes change with that choice.
  • The receptive day of a natural-cycle series is the day matching the mouse's separately deposited receptive session, since the files do not mark it and the female's behaviour is not annotated on those days.
  • Behaviour claims use 69 distinct annotated trials from 23 mice, where the paper has 74 from 28.
  • The GLM uses lags in 1-s steps, contiguous folds and a penalty chosen by cross-validation within each training set (the outcome changes with this choice; the last fifth of the training set breaks the ordering); choice probability compares a behaviour with every other bin of the interaction (pairs of behaviours, as in the Methods, are shown as a variant); the ACHW follows the authors' code. None of these is fixed by the Methods. Under contiguous folds an intercept-only model already scores below zero, so the GLM numbers are a weak test of Figure 2e.
  • The weights are applied to the stored, z-scored traces of each day. The per-mouse files' own traces were processed differently (cell i correlates with cell i at a median of 0.80 to 0.86), but the cell order matches and the projections from the two correlate at 0.94 to 0.96.

What this attempt found about the dandiset¶

  • It holds the imaging and annotations behind Figures 1, 2 and 5, and the male-inhibition sessions of Figure 4, but no rSLDS fits or latent factors beyond the per-cell weights of two mice, though its description says it contains latent factors. The VMHvl inhibition sessions of Figure 3h-k are not in it.
  • The per-mouse file labelled m542 holds the neural data of mouse 543 (72 cells; its traces match 543's receptive day cell by cell), and mouse 543 is labelled 543 in some files and m543 in another.
  • The same recording appears under two experiments several times: m764's natural-cycle day 1 is its primed ovariectomy session; m776's primed session has the same traces as its male-inhibition session; and day 3 of the ovariectomy series of m438, m541 and m551 has the same traces as the mouse's primed session. In four of these the annotations differ; in m438 the annotated interaction lasts 290.7 s in one file and 274.6 s in the other.
  • Which natural-cycle days were receptive is not recorded, and the female's behaviour is not annotated on most of them. The paper's subsets (4 of 7 natural-cycle mice, 4 of 8 male-inhibition mice, 50 oestrogen trials where 42 are deposited) are not identified.
  • The imaging metadata describe a two-photon microscope at 920 nm where the paper used a one-photon miniscope, the raw traces are labelled lumens, the z-scored traces are not z-scored per file, the image masks are 1 by 1 pixel, and experimenter, lab, institution and session dates are placeholders.
